scope_point_source_controls: Publication is Accredited Official Statistics.
Published series covers 2005 through 2024.
Statistics provide UK local-authority and regional greenhouse-gas estimates.
Primary national sources include the NAEI and DESNZ sub-national energy statistics.
A machine-readable local-authority CSV is published with the release.
The dataset spatially disaggregates territorial CO2, CH4 and N2O emissions.
The principal reporting basis is end user rather than only direct source location.
Fuel-production, fuel-processing and electricity-production emissions are reallocated to final energy users under the end-user approach.
Sector-specific disaggregation methods differ according to available data quantity and quality.
Activity inputs include DESNZ gas and electricity statistics, environmental-regulator data, large-installation point sources, NAEI high-resolution mapping and UKCEH LULUCF data.
National end-user emissions are used to derive activity emission factors.
Local-authority activity data are multiplied by relevant emission factors to estimate LA emissions.
The LA dataset and the national GHG inventory are subject to continuous improvement.
Population is used as an allocation variable for selected emission categories.
Population time series use census-based mid-year estimates where available.
Inter-census population estimates use dynamic-population-model trends to maintain time-series consistency.
The UK GHG Inventory is compiled annually under the NAEI programme on behalf of DESNZ.
The national inventory uses international best-practice inventory guidance and multiple official or sector-specific datasets.
The UK GHG Inventory supports annual UNFCCC reporting and domestic/international target assessment.
A common base of activity data and consistent methods are used across the NAEI programme.
NAEI sectors distinguish energy producers, energy users and other non-energy emission sources.
CH4 and N2O are converted to CO2-equivalent using the global-warming-potential basis stated in the technical report.
End-user reallocation is iterative where fuel producers consume outputs from other fuel producers.
The iterative end-user calculation terminates after fuel-producer emissions have been reallocated to end users.
CO2 from biofuel combustion is excluded from presented totals in line with inventory reporting rules.
Non-CO2 greenhouse-gas emissions from biofuel combustion remain included.
Landfill emissions are uniquely reallocated toward the location that produced the waste using biological-waste mass data.
Aviation, shipping and military-transport emissions are excluded from LA allocation because no clear local allocation basis is available.
Fluorinated gases are excluded where suitable local-level allocation data are unavailable.
Large industrial installations are mapped using the NAEI point-source database.
Industrial end-user estimates add an increment for emissions associated with processing fuels used at installations.
Point-source evidence includes 2005-2024 fuel information from installations in UK ETS or EU ETS regulatory datasets.
Point-source evidence also includes GHG emissions reported under IPPC/Pollution Inventory regimes.
Trade-association and operator data may supplement regulatory datasets for point-source fuel-use development.
Point-source sectors include power stations, refineries and coke ovens.
Point-source sectors include combustion plant regulated under IPC/IPPC.
Integrated steelworks are treated as a dedicated point-source sector.
Cement-clinker manufacture is included in point-source estimation.
Lime manufacture is included in point-source estimation.
Other sites with ETS annual-emissions data can be represented as point sources.
Energy-supply and fuel-production emissions are not retained solely at the physical emission point in the end-user dataset.
Direct ETS fuel and emissions data are checked against inventory classifications and DUKES fuel-consumption information.
ETS-to-IPPC installation relationships are established to reduce double counting of emissions and fuel consumption.
Reporting gaps are reviewed to distinguish real inactivity from reporting-threshold, scope, closure or replacement effects.
Operator and ETS data introduce some differences from the UK GHGI because national inventories rely on official fuel-use totals.
The technical report estimates operator-data use changes national carbon-emission estimates by less than one percent of the UK total.
Installation-specific operator data are preferred where they provide better fuel detail at individual industrial or commercial sites.
By-source point data receive an end-user increment for fuel-production emissions where appropriate.
Residual uncertainty remains in mapping relationships between ETS and IPPC installations even after reconciliation.
Point-source time series are actively checked for year-to-year consistency and may be revised when improved evidence becomes available.
uncertainty_mapping_controls: LA total-emission uncertainty combines national-emission uncertainty, spatial-distribution uncertainty and the sector contribution within each LA.
2024 LA uncertainties are propagated using a sum-of-squares method.
LULUCF net-emission uncertainties are excluded from the principal comparison because they can dominate the overall uncertainty signal.
Including LULUCF can at least double uncertainty for more than a dozen local authorities and can be much larger in extreme cases.
National inventory uncertainty uses Monte Carlo simulation.
Monte Carlo uncertainty assigns probability distributions to emission factors and activity data.
Local-sector national percentage errors are derived using weighted combinations of national-inventory sector errors.
Spatial-distribution uncertainties are acknowledged as difficult to quantify directly.
Expert elicitation is used where numerical spatial uncertainty data are unavailable.
DESNZ gas and electricity datasets provide a notable exception where quantitative location-related uncertainty information exists.
Correct allocation of meter locations to local authorities is an explicit contributor to gas/electricity geographical uncertainty.
Estimated meter readings and domestic-versus-non-domestic classification thresholds are additional uncertainty factors.
Mapped point sources are generally expected to be more geographically accurate than area-source estimates.
Area sources rely on surrogate datasets whose quality varies by sector and geography.
The methodology explicitly seeks the highest-quality available mapping data within practical constraints.
Some surrogate statistics are acknowledged as imperfect for allocating emissions spatially.
Large gas users, wastes, biomass and non-fuel industrial emissions can have relatively low geographical uncertainty where source locations are well reported.
Road-transport uncertainty is affected by sample and survey data used for vehicle movements and emission factors.
Average daily flows and average speeds do not capture all within-day or within-year traffic variation.
Minor-road modelling often uses regional average flows and speeds because direct observations are sparse.
Agriculture and waste CH4/N2O estimates carry greater process uncertainty than many CO2 estimates.
Small-industry coal and liquid-fuel distributions are assigned high uncertainty because local fuel-use distributions are poorly known.
The method does not infer local renewable consumption or energy-efficiency corrections to fill gaps in DESNZ gas/electricity datasets.
LA-specific sector emission amounts, rather than a UK-average sector mix, are used when combining uncertainties.
Median England LA uncertainty for 2024 excluding LULUCF is reported as plus or minus 4.6 percent.
Median England LA uncertainty for 2024 including LULUCF is reported as plus or minus 5.3 percent.
Median UK LA-level uncertainty excluding LULUCF is reported as plus or minus 4.8 percent.
Median UK LA-level uncertainty including LULUCF is reported as plus or minus 5.6 percent.
Protected Landscapes have materially higher median uncertainty than ordinary LA aggregates.
The 2024 UK GHG Inventory total uncertainty is reported as plus or minus 2.7 percent.
Great Britain road mapping uses Ordnance Survey Open Roads as a base network.
Northern Ireland road mapping uses road-network data from Ordnance Survey of Northern Ireland/Land and Property Services.
Road fuel-consumption factors depend on urban status, road type and speed-limit information.
Where minor-road speed-limit data are not available, the methodology uses stated urban and rural assumptions.
Major-road traffic flows are based on census count-point information.
Annual Average Daily Flow values are expanded to annual flows.
Seasonal expansion factors are used to account for seasonal variation in traffic counts.
Northern Ireland major-road count coverage is less dense than Great Britain coverage.
Some Northern Ireland count points provide total vehicles rather than vehicle-type splits, requiring an average vehicle split.
Northern Ireland traffic counts are assigned using spatial proximity and shared road number.
Great Britain count-point allocation combines shared road number with spatial proximity to the represented road section.
Simplified DfT count-point coverage lines support automated assignment of counts to the road network.
Road segments crossing LA boundaries are split so each segment can be assigned to the relevant LA.
Automated major-road traffic allocation is followed by manual checking and verification.
Most minor roads do not have link-by-link traffic-flow observations.
Available minor-road observations are used where present to improve mapping accuracy.
Most minor-road flows are modelled with regional average flows and vehicle-fleet mix.
County-level vehicle-kilometre estimates are used to improve consistency between NAEI mapping and DfT modelling.
Industrial sectors can combine explicit point-source estimates with area-source distributions.
Residual national emissions after subtracting point-source totals can be distributed as area sources using high-resolution postcode-level employment and fuel-use modelling.
